subject: Anthropology
title: Power and Authority
description: A 60-second lesson on Power and Authority.

hook.text: A thief uses power. A judge uses authority. Both control others, but only one has legitimacy. What's the difference?

buildup.text: Power is the ability to impose your will on others. Authority is power that people accept as legitimate and right.

discovery.text: Weber named three types: traditional (custom), charismatic (personal magnetism), and rational-legal (formal rules).

twist.text: Authority can shift. A charismatic leader dies, and the movement must find new grounds for legitimacy or collapse.

climax.text: Power without authority breeds resistance. Authority without power becomes hollow. Every society balances the two.

quiz.question: How does authority differ from power?
options: Authority is power that people accept as legitimate

details.summary: Power is the ability to influence others, while authority is power recognized as legitimate by the community. Max Weber identified three types of authority — traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal — each resting on different sources of legitimacy.
details.whyItMatters: The distinction between power and authority is fundamental to understanding political stability. Rulers who have power without authority rely on coercion; those with authority rule through consent, making governance more sustainable.
takeaways: Power is the ability to influence; authority is legitimized power
Weber identified traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal authority
Authority based on consent is more stable than coercion-based power

faq.question: What are Weber's three types of authority?
faq.answer: Traditional authority rests on longstanding customs and hereditary succession. Charismatic authority derives from a leader's personal qualities and perceived extraordinary abilities. Rational-legal authority rests on codified rules and bureaucratic procedures applied impartially.

faq.question: Can someone have power without authority?
faq.answer: Yes. Warlords, criminal organizations, and occupying forces exercise power without community recognition of their right to rule. This power relies on coercion and is inherently unstable because it must be constantly enforced rather than voluntarily accepted.
